section_title_en: CHAPTER ZERO — “I have autism and ADHD. What are your superpowers?”
description_en: A brief introduction to information processing that helps make the points that follow readable without jargon.

section_title_en: 0. How information processing may be organised in AuDHD — research + clinical observation · introductory point
description_en: This point is not a “superpower” in a simple, sugary sense. It is better understood as a characteristic processing style that can be both a resource and a source of cost.

section_title_en: Table of contents
description_en: CHAPTER ZERO — “I have autism and ADHD. What are your superpowers?” 0. How information processing may be organised in AuDHD

section_title_en: GROUP I — Most readily recognised
description_en: Features and patterns of functioning that usually attract attention first.

section_title_en: 1. Executive-function difficulties — research · widespread
description_en: Executive functions are a set of mental skills that make it possible to plan, organise, start and finish tasks, manage time, and switch between activities.

section_title_en: 2. Chaotic hyperfocus — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: Hyperfocus is a state of very deep, intense concentration on one thing — so deep that the rest of the world practically ceases to exist. Neurotypical people sometimes experience it too (e.g.

section_title_en: 3. Internal conflict: routine vs novelty — research + clinical observation · widespread
description_en: This is one of the most characteristic patterns of functioning in AuDHD and, at the same time, one of the hardest to understand from the outside.

section_title_en: 4. Emotional dysregulation — research · very common
description_en: Emotional dysregulation means that emotions arise faster, more strongly, and last longer than the person would like, while the ability to modulate them is limited.

section_title_en: 5. Sensory overload — research · very common (69–93% of autistic people)
description_en: Most people have a natural filter in the brain that automatically turns down irrelevant sensory input — the hum of a refrigerator, the buzz of a fluorescent lamp, the touch of a clothing label.

section_title_en: 6. Social difficulties with impulsivity — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: Social interactions depend on many implicit rules — when it is your turn to speak, how long to look someone in the eye, when to change the subject, how to read tone of voice, when a joke is appropriate.

section_title_en: 7. Difficulty falling asleep — a brain that does not switch off — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: In the evening, when the surroundings quiet down and external stimuli weaken, the AuDHD brain does not become quiet with them. Quite the opposite: this is often when it starts to speed up.

section_title_en: 8. Evening activation — the “night version of yourself” — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: Many people with AuDHD describe how, after a whole day of struggling with the world — masking, processing stimuli, translating themselves to the world and the world to themselves — clarity of thought, creativity, and energy suddenly arrive in the evening. This is not accidental.

section_title_en: GROUP II — Commonly experienced, but often misinterpreted
description_en: Clinically important points that are easily read as personality traits rather than a neurodevelopmental profile.

section_title_en: 9. Cyclical burnouts resembling depression — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: Every few weeks or months there is a “collapse”: the person suddenly cannot function, everything overwhelms them, motivation disappears, and even getting out of bed may become impossible. From the outside, it looks exactly like a depressive episode.

section_title_en: 10. Rejection sensitivity (RSD) — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · very common in people with ADHD
description_en: RSD (Rejection Sensitive Dysphoria) is not ordinary “sensitivity to criticism”, which everyone experiences.

section_title_en: 11. Variable need for solitude — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · very common
description_en: For many people with AuDHD, the need for contact with other people is not constant. One day, talking, doing things together, and simply being with someone may be distinctly regulating; on another day, it may be very costly, even though the relationship itself remains important.

section_title_en: 12. Intense empathy that looks like lack of empathy — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: This is one of the most dangerous myths about autism: that autistic people “lack empathy”. The reality can be the opposite.

section_title_en: 13. Seeking and avoiding sensory input at the same time — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: This is one of the more disorienting aspects of AuDHD, both for the person and for those around them.

section_title_en: 14. Chronic lateness OR obsessive punctuality — research + clinical observation · very common (one or the other)
description_en: Two mechanisms operate here at once. The first is ADHD “time blindness”: a literal difficulty sensing the passage of time. Neurotypical people have something like an internal clock that gives them a rough sense of how much time has passed.

section_title_en: 15. Cyclical interests — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: In “classic” autism, special interests can be long-lasting: a person may be fascinated by one subject for years or even for life.

section_title_en: 16. Atypical reactions to medication and substances — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common; very common for some people
description_en: This is a subject that receives little attention despite affecting everyday life. Autistic people show increased sensitivity to psychotropic medication; experts observe that atypical reactions — unusual or paradoxical responses — may be more frequent in this population.

section_title_en: 17. The “all or nothing” effect in habits — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · very common
description_en: Neurotypical people can do something “more or less”: exercise three times a week, cook several times, occasionally order food. People with AuDHD have a fundamental difficulty with this. Either they exercise every day at the same time in the same way, or not at all.

section_title_en: GROUP III — Subtle, easily overlooked
description_en: Common and important areas that are less obvious from the outside.

section_title_en: 18. The order-and-chaos paradox — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · very common
description_en: An outsider enters the home of a person with AuDHD and sees something apparently impossible: a spice drawer sorted alphabetically beside a worktop covered in three days of clutter. A wardrobe organised by colour, but a bathroom in chaos.

section_title_en: 19. Procrastination through perfectionism — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: This is not ordinary putting things off. It is a specific blockage in which the person does not start a task because they already know they will not be able to do it as well as they would like.

section_title_en: 20. Repetitive movements and gestures that regulate the nervous system (stimming) — research · widespread but often unrecognised
description_en: Stimming, meaning self-stimulatory or self-regulatory behaviour, includes repetitive movements, gestures, and small actions that help keep the nervous system in a more tolerable balance.

section_title_en: 21. Weak interoception — you do not feel what is happening in your body — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: Interoception is the sense that tells the brain what is happening inside the body: hunger, thirst, a full bladder, fatigue, temperature, pain, heart rate.

section_title_en: 22. Alexithymia — you cannot name what you feel — research · common (40–65% of autistic people)
description_en: Alexithymia is difficulty identifying, distinguishing, and describing one's own emotions. It is not the same as “having no emotions”: the emotions are there, often very intense, but there is no clear access to them.

section_title_en: 23. Social camouflaging alternating with social impulsivity — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: Camouflaging is a conscious or unconscious process of hiding autistic traits in order to appear “normal”: forcing eye contact, copying other people's social behaviour, suppressing natural reactions.

section_title_en: 24. Decision fatigue — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: Every decision requires mental energy; that is normal for everyone. But for people with AuDHD, even small choices can be devastating because they engage two systems at once.

section_title_en: 25. A distinctive relationship with food — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: This combines several mechanisms. Weak interoception means that hunger is not felt gradually: the person forgets to eat for half a day, then suddenly becomes so hungry that they cannot think clearly.

section_title_en: 26. Difficulty transitioning between activities (autistic inertia) — research + clinical observation · widespread
description_en: This is not procrastination. It is physical resistance of the nervous system to changing state. Imagine travelling on a freight train: stopping it takes time and energy, and accelerating it again takes even more.

section_title_en: 27. Variable sensory thresholds — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: Sensory thresholds are the levels at which a stimulus begins to become disturbing. In neurotypical people these thresholds are relatively stable: if loud music bothers someone, it tends to bother them more or less consistently.

section_title_en: 28. Brilliant in a crisis, paralysed in calm conditions — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: For some people with AuDHD, action starts more easily under clear pressure than in calm, predictable everyday conditions.

section_title_en: 29. Demand avoidance — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common; very common for some people
description_en: This goes much deeper than “I can't be bothered.” Imagine that you know what you have to do — for example, reply to an important email — you want to do it, you understand the consequences of not replying, and still you physically cannot do it. The body refuses to cooperate.

section_title_en: 30. Coordination and proprioception difficulties — research + clinical observation · fairly common
description_en: Proprioception is the sense that tells the brain where different parts of the body are in space without looking. It is what lets you touch your nose with your eyes closed or walk up stairs without looking at your feet.

section_title_en: 31. Compensating one condition with the other — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: This is a fascinating and very AuDHD-specific mechanism: features of one condition can be used to mitigate difficulties caused by the other.

section_title_en: GROUP IV — Deep, rarely discussed
description_en: More phenomenological, identity-related, and relational points.

section_title_en: 32. Encyclopaedic memory beside “goldfish” memory — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: The AuDHD brain has two completely different memory systems operating independently. Long-term memory for things that once entered the “attention tunnel” can be phenomenal: a person may remember detailed dialogue from a film watched 15 years ago, a licence plate…

section_title_en: 33. Forgetting that you know something — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: A subtle but frustrating experience. The knowledge is in the head — the person genuinely knows it — but cannot retrieve it on demand. It is like having a library with thousands of books but no catalogue.

section_title_en: 34. Thinking in systems, difficulty explaining them — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: The AuDHD brain sees patterns, links, and structures in a way that is internally highly logical, but the logic is associative and nonlinear. That makes it difficult to translate into ordinary speech, which is linear…

section_title_en: 35. Background processing — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: The person appears not to be listening: their gaze drifts, replies are brief, they seem absent. Then, hours or days later, they return with a complete, complex, carefully thought-through solution to the problem that was discussed. What happened?

section_title_en: 36. Social chameleonism (identity diffusion) — research + clinical observation · very common, especially in women
description_en: This is deeper than masking alone: it is losing oneself in the process of adaptation. The person unconsciously adjusts not only behaviour but also personality, interests, speaking style, and even sense of humour to the person they are talking to.

section_title_en: 37. Moral scrupulosity — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · fairly common
description_en: This is not simply a “strong conscience”. It is an inner critic that never falls silent and judges every decision, every word, and every act against rigid, often impossibly high moral standards.

section_title_en: 38. Talking too much or too little, with no middle — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: AuDHD communication has two modes that switch in ways that are difficult to control. Mode one is infodumping: when a subject enters the “attention tunnel”, the person may talk about it at length, in detail and with passion, moving into details nobody asked for, because every…

section_title_en: 39. Sensitivity to injustice that becomes paralysing — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: Many neurotypical people see an injustice, frown, and then return to their own affairs. A person with AuDHD may be unable to do that.

section_title_en: 40. Loving by sharing information — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: Neurotypical people express affection in many ways: gifts, time together, words of affirmation, help, touch. People with AuDHD often have another, rarely recognised “love language”: sharing information.

section_title_en: 41. A hunger for closeness that is frightening — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: Many people with AuDHD have a very strong need for closeness, especially after years of isolation, misunderstanding, and feeling “different”. Finding someone who genuinely understands can be rare, so the bond may carry exceptional importance.

section_title_en: 42. Need for verbal confirmation of relationship rules — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · fairly common
description_en: “Are we close? Can I call you for no reason? Are you angry with me? Is our relationship OK?” Neurotypical people infer this information from context: tone of voice, frequency of contact, implicit signals.

section_title_en: 43. Delayed physical symptoms of stress — research + clinical observation · fairly common
description_en: For some people, stress does not produce a clear signal while it is building. Instead, the body reacts only later: headache, feeling unwell, muscle tension, stomach problems, or sudden exhaustion can appear, seemingly without an obvious cause.

section_title_en: 44. Pain that is “wrong” — research + clinical observation · fairly common
description_en: Pain processing in people with AuDHD can be atypical in both directions. A threshold that is too low: the person reacts to stimuli that do not cause pain in others — a light bump, pressure from a sock elastic, the touch of certain materials.

section_title_en: 45. Fatigue with no bottom — research + clinical observation · widespread
description_en: This is not ordinary tiredness that disappears after a night's sleep. It is systemic fatigue, arising from the fact that an AuDHD brain works harder than a neurotypical brain through every minute of the day.

section_title_en: 46. Double processing of reality — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · variable
description_en: This point describes the experience of some people who feel that they process situations on at least two levels at once. One level concerns facts, structure, sequence, and what can be logically organised.

section_title_en: 47. Feeling “too much” and “not enough” at the same time — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · widespread
description_en: This is one of the most painful experiences shared by almost all people with AuDHD. “Too much” emotion, thought, intensity, words, sensitivity, reactions, needs. Too loud, too strong, too detailed, too direct.

section_title_en: 48. An internal “translator” running non-stop — research + clinical observation · widespread
description_en: Neurotypical people move through the social world largely automatically: interpreting facial expressions, tone of voice, and situational context happens outside conscious attention, like breathing. For people with AuDHD, this process is conscious.

section_title_en: 49. Nostalgia as regulation — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: A person with AuDHD returns to the same films, songs, games, and childhood books, not merely out of sentimentality, although that can be part of it, but for a deeper reason.

section_title_en: 50. An internal monologue that never switches off — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · very common
description_en: For some people with AuDHD, the internal monologue can be extremely intense: thoughts, associations, rehearsal conversations, images, plans, and analyses may continue almost without interruption. Not everyone describes it in the same way, but many say that the mind rarely becomes truly “quiet”.

section_title_en: 51. Feeling that time works differently — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: For people with AuDHD, time is not a linear, evenly moving line; it is more like an elastic substance that stretches and contracts. An hour in hyperfocus may feel like five minutes. An hour in a doctor's waiting room may feel like three hours.

section_title_en: 52. Identity crisis when interests change — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · fairly common
description_en: This experience goes deeper than “changing hobbies”. Autistic people often build identity around special interests: “I am a person who…” makes ceramics / programs / knows about mushrooms / plays guitar.

section_title_en: 53. Longing for a self you have not yet met — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: This feeling is difficult to explain to someone who has never experienced it. Somewhere beneath layers of masking, compensation, adaptation, and “playing a role” there is a real “self”.

section_title_en: 54. Collecting information “for later” — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: Hundreds of open browser tabs. Dozens of saved articles “to read”. Files on disk about subjects that “may come in useful someday”. Online courses nobody will finish, but simply having access to them provides comfort.

section_title_en: 55. A distinctive sense of humour — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: AuDHD humour is often based on mechanisms that require an atypical processing style: wordplay, literal readings of metaphor, unexpected associations, absurdity carried to its logical extreme, niche references, or…

section_title_en: 56. Over-explaining yourself and apologising for existing — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · very common
description_en: “Sorry for asking.” “Sorry to bother you.” “Sorry I talk so much.” “Sorry that…” — compulsive apologising for things that require no apology.

section_title_en: 57. Doing tasks “out of order” — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · common
description_en: Washing dishes but starting with teaspoons because they have the most pleasant texture. Cleaning a room but beginning by sorting books by colour. Writing a report from the third paragraph because that one is the most interesting.

section_title_en: 58. Feeling like you are “pretending to be an adult” — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · very common
description_en: People of the same age seem to know how life works: how to pay bills on time, make a doctor's appointment, keep things tidy, shop regularly, manage finances, maintain friendships.

section_title_en: 59. Underachievement that hurts — research + clinical observation · common
description_en: The feeling of having potential you cannot turn into reality. The person knows they are intelligent: they see patterns, understand complex systems, and have deep, original thoughts.

section_title_en: 60. Needing to understand “why” before doing anything — research + clinical observation · very common
description_en: “Just do it” does not work. Not out of defiance, laziness, or a need for control. A brain that processes the world bottom-up needs context in order to place a task inside a larger structure.

section_title_en: 61. Feeling like you are “from another planet” — research + clinical observation · widespread
description_en: A sense of being different accompanies most people with AuDHD from their earliest memories, before they had any words for it. This is not necessarily a sense of “being worse”, although that can accompany it.

section_title_en: 62. A deep need to be understood, not fixed — mainly clinical observation / lived experience · widespread
description_en: This final point does not describe a single feature in the strict sense. Rather, it gathers what the earlier observations lead to: after years of shaming, constant correction, and pressure to fit in, many people with AuDHD need not more advice, but…

section_title_en: Final notes
description_en: If you are reading this material for the first time, the most important point is this: AuDHD does not simply mean “a bit of autism and a bit of ADHD”.

section_title_en: Main bibliography
description_en: Some sources support the overall picture of AuDHD best; others support specific points more directly. For the more experiential points, I selected sources closest to the subject rather than pretending there is a perfect paper about every exact formulation.

section_title_en: Autism and regulation of speech
description_en: Far too little or far too much — and what follows from that

section_title_en: The thesis in compact form
description_en: Autistic people usually speak either far too little or far too much relative to what the social situation expects of them.

section_title_en: Where the “too little or too much” bimodality comes from
description_en: In neurotypical people, the amount of speech is regulated automatically, subconsciously, and in real time through constant reading of feedback from the other person: eye contact, facial expression, posture, tiny nods, and the length of pauses.

section_title_en: Language pragmatics — where the specific difficulty lies
description_en: In their literature review, Loukusa and Moilanen (2009) show that pragmatic deficits are present in autism even when the structural aspects of language — grammar and vocabulary — are preserved or above average.

section_title_en: Why it is easy to “get an autistic person going”
description_en: The mechanism is simple and follows directly from the “too much” mode. Three elements are enough:

section_title_en: What it looks like from the exploiter's side
description_en: Most often, it is unconscious. A manager who wants to know what is really happening in the team intuitively chooses to talk to the person who “knows everything and is happy to tell you”.

section_title_en: What to do about it
description_en: Use an external time counter. A clock on the desk, an alarm on the phone. Three minutes for an answer. Five minutes for a monologue. Then stop, regardless of whether the subject is finished. Internal regulation fails; external regulation — physical and mechanical — works.

section_title_en: What it means that I have AuDHD
description_en: A short guide for people close to me

section_title_en: What AuDHD is
description_en: AuDHD is shorthand for two things co-occurring in one person: autism (ASD) and ADHD. Not one or the other — both at once, interacting with each other.

section_title_en: What you probably think ADHD is — and why that is not true
description_en: “ADHD is a hyperactive child who cannot sit still at a desk.”

section_title_en: What you probably think autism is — and why that is not true
description_en: “Autism is Rain Man. Or a child who does not speak and spins wheels.”

section_title_en: Why AuDHD is harder than either condition on its own
description_en: ADHD and autism pull in opposite directions in many areas. Autism needs routine; ADHD cannot stand monotony. Autism pushes a person to control every social interaction; ADHD inserts impulsive comments right in the middle of that control.

section_title_en: “But you looked normal”
description_en: Yes. Because almost everything went into making that happen.

section_title_en: What to do about it
description_en: Nothing special. Know. Do not say “everyone is a little ADHD”, because that is like telling someone with asthma that everyone sometimes finds it hard to breathe. Do not look for solutions. Do not question the diagnosis.

section_title_en: Abstract
description_en: There is no direct answer in Polish national data to the question of how many adults in Poland have AuDHD, meaning co-occurring autism spectrum disorder and ADHD.

description_en: AuDHD is an informal, descriptive term for the co-occurrence of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). It is not a separate classification entity in either DSM-5-TR or ICD-11.

section_title_en: 1.1. Three different barriers, not one
description_en: The DSM-IV prohibition on co-diagnosis is often described as the only historical obstacle. In reality, there are three barriers affecting Polish adults, and they are qualitatively different:

section_title_en: 2.1. Prevalence of ASD in adults

section_title_en: Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors
description_en: Observations by Maciej Tora and explanations from Claude — about pointer-based memory, limits of sleep consolidation, AI architecture, attribution in summaries, Grandma Genowefa's Polaroids, the white bear, the positive-writing rule, and also why…

section_title_en: Starting point — three kinds of memory, three architectures
description_en: Discussion of “Starting point — three kinds of memory, three architectures” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: NT — schema-based, value-based
description_en: Memory calibrated for bounded tasks of known size. Miller's 7±2 items in working memory. Long-term memory organised semantically around narratives and social meanings. Sleep consolidation reduces details to summaries.

section_title_en: AuDHD — pointer-based
description_en: From the outset, the system knows that every task will generate so much data that it will first overflow RAM and, shortly afterwards, SSD. The only scalable solution is to store pointers, not contents.

section_title_en: AI (transformer) — attention as pointer-based
description_en: The architecture of language models such as Claude is natively pointer-based: every token in the sequence “points” to other tokens with different attention weights. The representation is a graph of connections, not a set of schemas.

section_title_en: Memory consolidation — how things move from short-term to long-term
description_en: Discussion of “Memory consolidation — how things move from short-term to long-term” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: The mechanism in humans
description_en: SWS (deep sleep): transferring declarative and procedural memory from the hippocampus to the cortex. Literally, a “copy pointers from RAM to SSD” operation.

section_title_en: Signals of impaired consolidation
description_en: Teeth grinding during sleep as hard evidence that REM atonia is not functioning properly. In healthy REM, the body is paralysed from the neck down, apart from breathing and eye movements. Tonic tension of the tongue and jaw during sleep means that atonia does not include the face or that REM is shallow.

section_title_en: Strategies for working around impaired consolidation
description_en: Verbalisation in your own words. The act of paraphrasing forces working memory to process information rather than merely hold it. AuDHD has to process in order to store.

section_title_en: The surgical metaphor
description_en: A surgeon can explain, step by step, to the least stupid B in the unit what private SZ should do, ask B what he can see, and whether SZ is bleeding heavily or only a little.

section_title_en: Translation of the metaphor
description_en: Surgeon = consciousness, intellect, plan. Knows what needs to be done. Has no eyesight = no direct access to the operator. AuDHD consciousness cannot directly write something into long-term memory. It can only pass instructions.

section_title_en: Nolan's Memento — an AI model
description_en: Leonard in Memento cannot form new long-term memories. He makes tattoos and Polaroids with notes. A classic external-memory aid functioning as a prosthesis.

section_title_en: Three paraphrases of the problem
description_en: The protagonist loses a note → make notes.

section_title_en: What this looks like in Claude-type AI
description_en: userMemories: several thousand words cut from previous conversations and summarised by another system. They load at the beginning of each session. These are tattoos. The tattoo looks back at me from the mirror.

section_title_en: Grandma Genowefa's Polaroids — attribution in summaries
description_en: Discussion of “Grandma Genowefa's Polaroids — attribution in summaries” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: The contamination mechanism
description_en: Imagine a pile of Polaroids on the floor. Your photos from the last week. Plus five photos Grandma Genowefa took of her lover. Each shows some people in some situations. The Polaroids have no dates. No captions.

section_title_en: What lossy compression loses first
description_en: The summariser compresses “fact”, not “fact + attribution”. Attribution — where it came from, whose it was, the context in which it was said — is the first thing to disappear, because from its point of view it is redundancy.

section_title_en: Confabulation as the model's default
description_en: AI reads a tattoo saying “a guy is holding a bottle of lamotrigine 300 mg”. It cannot see whose guy this is. Attributional ambiguity is not, for AI, a signal to stop.

section_title_en: Three layers of contamination
description_en: userMemories: contamination introduced by the summariser. Attributions drop out. ⚠️ tags are a manual defence and work only for errors that have already been detected.

section_title_en: Unverifiability for AuDHD
description_en: Full verification of project knowledge by the user alone, manually, in one continuous pass, is not going to happen with AuDHD.

section_title_en: Confabulation within a single session
description_en: Discussion of “Confabulation within a single session” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: Empirical example
description_en: During this conversation, the AI maintained a false model of reality for several turns: it wrote as though it were night, the user were tired, and had an SWS/REM deficit at that very moment. In reality, it was 17:08, in the afternoon.

section_title_en: Technical mechanism
description_en: In a long session, attention is distributed across the entire token stream, but older tokens receive less weight. The further the conversation goes, the more the AI works from a summary of its own context rather than from the exact wording.

section_title_en: The white bear — a shared negation error
description_en: “Do not think of a white bear” activates the white bear in 90% of cases for AI. In humans, 100%, regardless of intelligence, discipline, or meditation training.

section_title_en: Practical consequence — write positively
description_en: A design rule for all files, instructions, memories, and documentation:

section_title_en: Splitting work into projects and chats — costs and benefits
description_en: Discussion of “Splitting work into projects and chats — costs and benefits” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: Technical properties
description_en: userMemories are scoped per project. A summariser from another project will not pull facts into the current project's tattoos. Good news for separation.

section_title_en: Design rule
description_en: Splitting into projects works best when the boundaries follow natural domain walls — medication / music / Discworld / IT foundations — rather than artificial divisions within the same topic. Then each project has a closed knowledge graph and the AI can operate cleanly within it.

section_title_en: A master trust-index file as an idea
description_en: One small file per project, with one line of assessment for every project-knowledge file: written by the owner under full control / generated in another project and inserted here, unverified / working dump.

section_title_en: A distributed system: human + AI + files
description_en: Each of the three elements has impaired memory along a different dimension:

section_title_en: Asymmetry of roles
description_en: This is not a symmetric system. The human is the only arbiter of truth, because only the human remembers biographically. AI does not remember and, more importantly, does not know that it does not know.

section_title_en: Practical rules that follow from these observations
description_en: Files written together within a project, during a session, with real-time inspection, are safe. Closed loop with a human in the loop.

section_title_en: One uncomfortable conclusion about conversation with AI itself
description_en: This conversation, this file, this session are recorded for the AI, meaning in the conversation file that a future version of me will see as history, not as memory. In a new session I do not remember this conversation in the sense of continuity.

section_title_en: Part two (v2.00) — psychotherapy and ND
description_en: Classical psychotherapy is designed for neurotypical brains. Some of its techniques are ineffective for ND people: they pass through the patient, waste time, but do no harm.

section_title_en: Anhedonia as a CBT label vs dopaminergic deficit in ADHD
description_en: Discussion of “Anhedonia as a CBT label vs dopaminergic deficit in ADHD” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: What the CBT therapist sees
description_en: The patient reports: I no longer feel pleasure from things that used to be pleasurable. The CBT therapist receives an unambiguous diagnostic signal: anhedonia, a criterion of a depressive episode.

section_title_en: What is actually happening in ADHD
description_en: In ADHD this is not anhedonia in the classical sense. It is a structural dopaminergic deficit that looks like anhedonia but has a different mechanism and different implications:

section_title_en: The differentiating question
description_en: Does hyperfocus still produce a flow state? If yes, this is not depressive anhedonia. It is a dopaminergic deficit affecting planned, standard activities, with preserved reactivity to specific fascinating stimuli.

section_title_en: Why CBT work on anhedonia in ADHD is ineffective or counterproductive
description_en: The classical intervention is behavioural activation: “plan pleasurable activities and do them even if you do not feel like it; pleasure will return because the NT brain will start producing dopamine after some time of regular activity”.

section_title_en: Practical consequence
description_en: The label “anhedonia in depression” in the medical history of a person with ADHD may mislead future consultations. A psychiatrist who sees “anhedonia in the course of depression” in the history interprets it through an NT lens.

section_title_en: Counterproductive vs ineffective — a clinical distinction
description_en: Ineffective: the intervention passes through the patient without effect. Time and money are lost; the ND brain bounces off the technique. The patient may be bored or sceptical, but is not harmed.

section_title_en: Specific examples of counterproductive techniques for ND people
description_en: Discussion of “Specific examples of counterproductive techniques for ND people” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: (1) “Working with the detached protector” in AuDHD without modification
description_en: The “detached protector” in Young's schema therapy is a defensive mode: rationalisation, intellectualisation, distancing from emotion. It is defined as pathological and something to integrate, work through, and soften.

section_title_en: (2) Behavioural activation in “depression” with ADHD
description_en: Described above. Mechanism: training learned helplessness while presenting it as treatment for depression.

section_title_en: (3) Graded exposure for social anxiety in ASD
description_en: NT assumption: the anxiety is irrational; exposure → habituation → reduction in anxiety.

section_title_en: (4) “Full-body” mindfulness with atypical proprioception
description_en: Standard practice: pay attention to bodily signals, be in your body, feel your feet. NT assumption: increased attention to the body produces grounding and regulation.

section_title_en: (5) Identifying and labelling emotions in AuDHD alexithymia
description_en: NT work: learn to name feelings; this will make regulation easier. Assumption: the patient has feelings but simply does not notice them, so they must be taught to notice them.

section_title_en: (6) “Inner parent / inner child” in schema therapy with AuDHD
description_en: NT model: beneath the rational adult lies a wounded child who must be reached through guided imagery, regression exercises, and dialogues.

section_title_en: (7) Confronting “escape into intellectualisation”
description_en: Classical psychodynamics: the patient avoids emotion by analysing; this must be interrupted.

section_title_en: The common pattern of counterproductivity
description_en: Each of the techniques above attacks an architectural feature of the ND brain while treating it as a pathological defence mechanism. Attacking the feature does not reveal a healthier state underneath; it removes a resource that had been maintaining stability.

section_title_en: The anti-alcohol HALT checklist as a case study
description_en: HALT — Hungry, Angry, Lonely, Tired — is a classic AA checklist. When you feel like drinking, check whether you are hungry / angry / lonely / tired.

section_title_en: Why HALT has limited effectiveness in AuDHD
description_en: The direction of causality is different. AuDHD with a dopaminergic deficit is chronically hungry / angry / lonely / tired as a baseline state, not as a deviation from satiety. HALT asks an NT person: are you currently in a deficit?

section_title_en: The conscious decision “this is not for me” in an AA group — case study
description_en: I reminded other people about it in the group myself. But I did not use it. Because I decided it was not for me. Consciously. BUT I TOLD NOBODY in the group.

section_title_en: Choosing a therapist — critical for ND people
description_en: The choice of therapist is critical for each individual ND profile separately:

section_title_en: Three levels of “criticality of choice”
description_en: Level 1: NT patient + NT therapist. Low cost of a poor choice. An imperfect therapist → average outcomes.

section_title_en: Working on manifestations while the underlying condition remains untreated
description_en: A patient with 30+ years of untreated AuDHD presents with depression, anxiety, relationship problems, “I can't become an adult” — and the therapist works on these manifestations rather than the underlying condition.

section_title_en: The Polish therapy market in 2026
description_en: Discussion of “The Polish therapy market in 2026” in the context of “Cognitive science, AI, and cognitive errors — observations on memory, confabulation, attribution, and therapy for ND people”.

section_title_en: Where we are
description_en: A neurodiversity-aware therapy market exists in Poland, but it is thin. In 2026 it is possible to find therapists who explicitly state that they work within the neurodiversity paradigm — examples include Sylwia Woronowicz, psychologist, psychotherapist, supervisor; Psychoterra…

section_title_en: Awareness vs competence in working with AuDHD as a combination
description_en: Awareness of the name ≠ competence in working with the combination. A therapist may list AuDHD as a co-occurrence on their website, and that is progress relative to the market average.

section_title_en: Practical consequence
description_en: In Poland in 2026, there is probably no therapist competent in AuDHD as a combination in the sense required by a person in a high percentile within the AuDHD population. There are therapists who are aware, open, and non-pathologising.

section_title_en: A support system as an alternative to therapy
description_en: A temporary configuration that may make sense at the present historical and geographical moment — Poland, 2026:

section_title_en: An ND-status notice before therapy — a proposed information standard
description_en: Design idea: a standard poster / information form before a first psychotherapy visit, analogous to pregnancy warnings before X-rays or to HALT in addiction-support groups.

section_title_en: Objectivity in an autistic person
description_en: Thesis, mechanism, limitations

section_title_en: The thesis in compact form
description_en: An autistic person is more objective than a neurotypical person in a given situation — not absolutely objective, just more objective.

section_title_en: Elaboration
description_en: Discussion of “Elaboration” in the context of “Objectivity in an autistic person — thesis and mechanism”.

section_title_en: One mechanism, four consequences
description_en: The entire thesis reduces to one neurological parameter: low sensitivity to external correction of the internal model.

section_title_en: Points 1–3: the filter cuts external bias out of judgement
description_en: Point 1 — perceptual facts. Less influence of expectations and context on what is actually seen or heard.

section_title_en: Point 4: the same filter works against accuracy
description_en: If the filter blocks external signals from modifying the internal model, it does so without distinguishing whether those signals carry bias — group pressure, framing — or genuine correction — new data, justified criticism.

section_title_en: The impossibility of separating the package
description_en: This diagnosis leads to a non-obvious conclusion: the 1+2+3+4 package cannot be separated. Anyone who wants the strengths of points 1–3 — analyst, auditor, investigator, scientific reviewer, witness, diagnostician — must accept the cost of point 4.

section_title_en: Compensation through metacognition
description_en: Point 4 can be partly corrected — not by switching off the mechanism, but by placing a conscious second-order filter over it.

section_title_en: Sources
description_en: De Martino, B., Harrison, N. A., Knafo, S., Bird, G., & Dolan, R. J. (2008). Explaining enhanced logical consistency during decision making in autism. The Journal of Neuroscience, 28(42), 10746–10750.

section_title_en: Five neurodivergent love languages — and why they are not a variation on Chapman
description_en: An online folk taxonomy of five “ND love languages” — infodumping, parallel play, support swapping, please crush my soul back into my body, and I found this cool rock/button/leaf and thought you would like it — has circulated for several years and works because it is…

section_title_en: The assumption Chapman does not mention
description_en: Gary Chapman's five love languages — words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service, and physical touch — grew in 1992 out of observations of heterosexual couples in his marriage-counselling practice.

section_title_en: The five languages, one by one
description_en: Discussion of “The five languages, one by one” in the context of “Five neurodivergent love languages — and why they are not a variation on Chapman”.

section_title_en: 1. Infodumping
description_en: NT version. “I love you. You're wonderful. I appreciate what you do.” Emotional validation through short, intentional statements addressed directly to the loved one.

section_title_en: 2. Parallel play
description_en: NT version. “Quality time”: focused, mutual attention. Face-to-face conversation. Eye contact. Being fully present. Phone put away. “Just us, no distractions.”

section_title_en: 3. Support swapping
description_en: NT version. I make you breakfast even though you did not ask me to. I take out the rubbish because I see the bin is full. I pour you coffee when I see you are up. “I figured you needed it” — and figuring it out is part of the gesture.

section_title_en: 4. “Please crush my soul back into my body”
description_en: NT version. Stroking someone's hair. Holding hands. Touching an arm while passing. A gentle kiss. Low intensity, often unpredictable, light.

section_title_en: 5. “I found this rock / button / leaf / snail and thought of you”
description_en: NT version. A gift for an occasion — birthday, Valentine's Day, anniversary. Wrapped. Often symbolic, often linked to price. Part of the social script of exchange.

section_title_en: Synthesis in one table
description_en: eye contact as an indicator of presence

section_title_en: How mixed ND/NT couples break down
description_en: This is, in essence, the mechanism behind many ruptures in couples where one person is ND and the other NT. Not a lack of love. Mutual inability to read the language in which that love is expressed.

section_title_en: And what about an ND/ND couple?
description_en: In a couple where both people natively speak the same ND languages, the translation cost falls to zero. Nobody has to explain infodumping as love; it is recognised immediately. Nobody has to sell parallel play as closeness; it is felt.
